title: Response to Husaka - CHEST - Bench vs Ring Push Ups
summary: A respectful response video to a commenter (Husaka) who argued that the bench press is all you need for chest. He agrees bench is the best horizontal press on risk/reward and progression, but argues ring push-ups add safe extra chest volume and frequency, a deeper stretch than the bench, joint-friendly freedom of movement and external rotation. He also disputes that chin-ups are best for biceps, defends squeeze/stretch and mind-muscle connection, and contrasts Pendlay rows with Coan rows.

claims.claim: He doesn't want a call-out or drama channel, but will always engage in intelligent discussion through response videos.
He does a lot of ring push-ups as an additional horizontal press for chest volume, considers them a great hypertrophy addition, and personally a must-do.
He only cares about hypertrophy, size and looks, not strength.
The bench is the best horizontal press because of its risk-to-reward ratio.
Weighted dips may stress the pecs more than bench because nothing catches you at the bottom, so you absorb all the kinetic energy (like squat vs box squat).
He wouldn't recommend dips over bench because some people can't do them safely, they carry higher shoulder injury risk, and progression is cumbersome with a dip belt.
Bench beats push-ups and ring push-ups for progression: with bodyweight you don't know the load, and adding vests or plates is annoying.
He's a heavy lifter and not advanced on rings (no planche push-ups or iron cross), but you don't need advanced ring skills; even beginners get good gains from entry-level ring movements.
Weighted push-ups are more risk than reward and awkward to set up.
On the bench you also don't know how much load your chest takes: grip and arch shift work to front delts and triceps, so 225 on the bar isn't 225 on the chest.
Bench moves more tonnage through the chest, but it doesn't necessarily give more overall chest activation than push-ups.
Bench ROM is arbitrary, set by body structure; ring push-ups allow more shoulder flexion and elbow travel, a deeper chest stretch, without the shoulder risk of a cambered bar.
Saying there are no must-do exercises but presenting the bench as king is contradictory; something being better doesn't mean it's the only thing you should do.
To maximise chest growth, hit the chest every 48 hours or at least three times a week.

High-frequency bench smokes his shoulders and then hurts his overhead press and even his squat because every shoulder-flexion movement becomes painful; most lifters are the same, and those who tolerate 10x10 heavy, frequent bench are outliers.

Shoulder injuries are the number one injury in retired powerlifters, even those with good form; he believes it comes largely from heavy horizontal pressing stressing the AC joint and rotator cuff, and is preventable.
Ring push-ups and push-ups don't carry over to bench strength: he was very advanced at push-ups yet benched only about 145 lbs his first time (while lightweight).
Push-ups are great for size and joint health but won't add much bench strength; strength and hypertrophy are different things.

Ring push-ups are extra horizontal pressing volume that is safer, can be done more frequently and consistently over long periods, and doesn't tax you; if you can match that volume with bench alone, do it, but most can't.
He has never seen someone who only did chin-ups develop elite biceps; compound movements can't tell you how much load goes to a given muscle.
He has about 18-inch arms, mostly biceps; he reached 16 inches without ever doing a chin-up, and chin-ups do little for his biceps.
At the bottom of a chin-up the back takes most of the stretch, and the biceps only engage fully near lockout; lifters who built big backs with chin-ups got little biceps growth.
EMG studies favouring compounds usually use novices, who gain more initially from heavy compounds; long term, isolation is king for specific body parts.
'Squeeze' and 'stretch' are no more buzzwords than 'concentric' and 'eccentric'; using scientific terms is often a way to intimidate and claim authority.

Loaded stretch creates hypertrophy (e.g. letting the traps stretch under a held weight), and different chest exercises stretch the fibres at different angles and elbow paths, a distinct stimulus that matters in bodybuilding.
He doesn't feel his quads when squatting and they still grow, but some movements only made muscles grow once he connected with them, and many people report the same.
Many people don't feel their chest on bench; flies or other squeeze/stretch work help them activate the chest better on the bench.
He prefers opinion-based discussion over pulling scientific data out of a hat; he finds it a healthier way to debate.
Pick exercises with a good stretch-to-risk ratio: ones that stretch fibres differently while staying safe, rather than heavy loads in deep stretch that risk tearing the muscle.
In a bodybuilding context, 'athletic' means moving your body through space: a pistol squat or push-up is athletic, a squat or bench is not.
He used to be the heavy guy strong on compounds and now wants to move better.
Rings are healthier for shoulders, wrists and elbows: lower load makes form and sensation easier to focus on, and the rings move freely so joints find their own path, unlike a fixed bar or floor.
On ring push-ups he opens the chest and squeezes the traps at the bottom, which gives external rotation rather than internal rotation, using more rear delt and upper traps.
Bench locks the body into one plane; grinding reps there can slowly erode mobility and build bad habits.
Instead of bar chest stretches, finish workouts with about five sets of deep ring push-ups, varying the elbow angle.
Pendlay rows are good for strength and size but lack stretch because you let the bar fall instead of catching it; lifts that are positive-only (like dumping a deadlift) are weaker for hypertrophy.
Coan rows let you catch the weight and lengthen the upper back, and allow more load than Pendlay rows.
English is his third language and he speaks four languages.
He works in IT and refuses Skype calls to protect his identity, since IP and personal data are easy to extract.

exercises.name: Ring push-ups
cues: rings elevated so you can go deep
open the chest and squeeze traps at the bottom (external rotation)
about 5 sets at end of workout
exercises.why: safe extra chest volume and frequency, deeper stretch, joint-friendly

exercises.name: Bench press
exercises.why: best horizontal press on risk/reward and progression, but limited ROM and shoulder-stressing at high frequency

exercises.name: Weighted dips
exercises.why: strong chest stimulus but higher shoulder risk and awkward progression

exercises.name: Cambered bar bench
exercises.why: deeper stretch but compromised shoulder position

exercises.name: Chin-ups
exercises.why: mostly back; little biceps growth for him

exercises.name: Coan row
exercises.why: stretch plus more load than Pendlay

viewer_questions: Is the bench press all you need for chest, or do ring push-ups add anything?
